meta.scope_sentence: Sample report for a fictional online shop. Every name, path, line of code and finding in it is invented to show the report format.
meta.stack: Node.js 22 with Express 5 and PostgreSQL · React 19 single-page app
meta.code_scope: 214 source files, about 18,600 lines (`api/` and `web/`), tests and generated code excluded
meta.endpoints: 41 HTTP routes in `api/src/routes/`, 1 payment webhook, 23 React screens
meta.integrations: Payment provider (webhook callbacks), transactional email service, object storage for product images

summary.reviewed: This deep review covered the Acme Shop API and its React storefront on branch `main`, ahead of the 2.5 release that opens the shop to guest checkout.
summary.urgent: Two problems need fixing before release. The API decodes admin tokens without checking their signature, so anyone can forge an admin session ({ref:jwt}). The payment webhook trusts any caller, so an attacker can mark an unpaid order as paid ({ref:webhook}).
summary.well_built: Database access is parameterised throughout, passwords are hashed with Argon2id, session cookies are `HttpOnly` and `SameSite=Lax`, and file uploads are type-checked and stored outside the web root.

layers.name: Backend
layers.controls_held: parameterised queries, Argon2id password hashing, upload type checks

layers.name: Web frontend
layers.controls_held: React output escaping outside one component, no secrets in the bundle

findings.title: Admin Token Signature Not Verified
findings.description: `requireAdmin` reads the bearer token with `jwt.decode`, which parses the token without checking its signature, and then trusts the `role` claim. Every route under `/api/admin` relies on this middleware.
attack: The attacker, with no account, builds a token with the payload `{"sub":"1","role":"admin"}` and any signature.
They send `GET /api/admin/customers` with that token in the `Authorization` header.
The middleware accepts the token and the API returns every customer record.
findings.impact: Full admin access without credentials: read and change every customer, order and product, and issue refunds.
findings.recommendation: Replace `jwt.decode` with `jwt.verify(token, config.jwtSecret, { algorithms: ['HS256'] })`, as `requireUser` already does in the same file. Add a test that a token signed with another key gets 401.

findings.title: Payment Webhook Accepts Unsigned Callbacks
findings.description: The payment webhook marks an order as paid from the `orderId` and `status` in the request body. It never checks the provider's `Payment-Signature` header, and the route is public so the provider can reach it.
attack: The attacker places an order and stops at the payment page.
They send `POST /api/webhooks/payment` with `{"orderId":"<their order>","status":"succeeded"}`.
The order moves to `paid` and is released for shipping.
findings.impact: Goods shipped without payment, for any order the attacker can create.
findings.recommendation: Verify the `Payment-Signature` header with the provider SDK's `constructEvent` and the webhook secret before reading the body, and re-fetch the payment from the provider by id before changing the order. Add a test that an unsigned callback gets 400 and leaves the order unchanged.

findings.title: Order Details Readable by Any Customer
findings.description: `GET /api/orders/:id` loads the order by id only. The query has no `customer_id` filter and the handler does not compare the owner with `req.user.id`. Order ids are sequential.
attack: The attacker signs up as an ordinary customer.
They request `GET /api/orders/1`, `/2`, `/3` and so on.
Each response returns another customer's name, delivery address, phone number and items.
findings.impact: Any customer can read every other customer's order history and personal data.
findings.recommendation: Load the order with `orders.findForCustomer(id, req.user.id)` (the helper the order list already uses) and return 404 when it finds nothing. Add a test that customer B gets 404 for customer A's order.

findings.title: Stack Traces Returned in Error Responses
findings.description: The global error handler sends `err.stack` to the client in every environment. A malformed request body is enough to trigger it.
attack: The attacker sends `POST /api/cart` with an invalid JSON body.
The response contains the full stack trace, with file paths and library versions.
findings.impact: Reveals internal paths, library versions and query fragments that help plan further attacks.
findings.recommendation: Return `{ error: 'internal_error', requestId }` to the client and log the stack server side with the same request id.

findings.title: Single-Use Coupon Redeemable Twice in a Race
findings.fact: The transaction isolation level used for `coupons.redeem` in production.
findings.safe_check: Run `SHOW default_transaction_isolation;` on a production read replica.
findings.description: `redeem` reads `used_at`, checks it is empty and then updates it in a separate statement. Two requests sent together can both pass the check. Whether this works depends on the database isolation level, which is not in the repository.
attack: The attacker holds one single-use coupon and two carts.
They send both checkout requests with the coupon at the same moment.
Both orders get the discount.
findings.impact: A single-use discount applied more than once. The loss per coupon is small, but the same pattern is easy to script.
findings.recommendation: Redeem with one conditional update, `UPDATE coupons SET used_at = now() WHERE code = $1 AND used_at IS NULL RETURNING id`, and reject the checkout when no row comes back. Add a test that fires two redemptions in parallel.
poc: const coupon = await db.one('SELECT * FROM coupons WHERE code = $1', [code]);
await db.none('UPDATE coupons SET used_at = now(), order_id = $2 WHERE id = $1', [coupon.id, orderId]);

findings.title: Stored XSS in Product Reviews
findings.description: Review text is rendered with `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` so that line breaks show. The API stores review text as submitted, so any customer can store markup that runs in other shoppers' browsers.
attack: The attacker, signed in as a customer, posts a review containing ``.
Another shopper opens the product page.
The script runs in the shopper's session and can act as them on the storefront.
findings.impact: Actions in a victim's session, such as changing the delivery address of an open order. The session cookie itself is `HttpOnly`.
findings.recommendation: Render the text as a React child and use CSS `white-space: pre-line` for line breaks. Add a test that a review containing `` renders as text.

findings.title: Refresh Token Kept in localStorage
findings.description: The storefront stores the long-lived refresh token in `localStorage`, where any script on the page can read it. Combined with {ref:xss}, an attacker could take the token and keep access after the victim leaves the page.
attack: The attacker gets script running on the storefront (for example through {ref:xss}).
The script reads `localStorage.refreshToken` and sends it to the attacker.
The attacker uses the token to get new access tokens for the victim's account.
findings.impact: Long-lived access to one customer's account. It needs a separate script-injection flaw first.
findings.recommendation: Have the API set the refresh token as an `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite=Strict` cookie scoped to `/api/auth/refresh`, and keep only the short-lived access token in memory.

findings.title: No Content Security Policy
findings.description: Neither the HTML nor the static host sends a `Content-Security-Policy`. A policy would not fix {ref:xss}, but it would stop an injected script from loading code or sending data to another host.
attack: No direct attack. This is hardening that limits what an injected script can do.
findings.impact: No direct impact today. Without a policy, any script injection has full reach.
findings.recommendation: Send `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; img-src 'self' https://images.acme.example; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'` from the static host, first in report-only mode.

assets_and_actors: Assets: customer accounts and personal data, orders and their payment state, coupons, and the admin console. Actors: anonymous visitors, signed-in customers, admins, and the payment provider calling the webhook.

threats.path: Script runs in another shopper's session

limitations: Infrastructure, the CDN and the static host configuration were not in scope. Response headers were judged from the repository only.
The production database isolation level could not be checked (see 5.2).
No dynamic testing was done. Every attack was traced in the code and checked by a second agent.
Ledger: 64 units, 61 `covered`, 3 `out_of_scope` (generated API client, Storybook stories, seed scripts).
not_applicable: OTP step-up and one-time proofs (no flow uses one), Card data protection (card entry is hosted by the payment provider)
secure_controls: Backend: every SQL query uses `pg` parameters, including dynamic sorting through an allow-list (`api/src/db/products.js:22`).
Backend: passwords are hashed with Argon2id and compared in constant time (`api/src/services/users.js:40`).
Backend: `requireUser` verifies token signature, expiry and algorithm (`api/src/middleware/auth.js:4-10`).
Backend: uploads are checked by content type and size and stored outside the web root (`api/src/routes/uploads.js:15`).
Web frontend: no API keys or secrets in the built bundle; `VITE_` variables hold public values only.
Web frontend: every other component renders user content through React escaping.

remediation.action: Verify the signature and algorithm of every token in `requireAdmin` (Backend).
Check the provider signature on the payment webhook and re-fetch the payment before changing an order (Backend).
Scope every order and address lookup to the signed-in customer (Backend).
Render review text as plain text and add a lint rule against `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` (Web frontend).
Move the refresh token to an `HttpOnly` cookie (Backend and Web frontend).
Return generic error bodies with a request id (Backend).
Make coupon redemption a single conditional update (Backend).
Add a Content Security Policy, first in report-only mode (Web frontend).

methodology.enumeration: `inventory.py` listed 41 routes, 1 webhook, 23 screens and 57 sinks across `api/` and `web/`; the coverage ledger tracked each one to a result.
methodology.dependencies: `npm audit` and gitleaks were run; neither reported an issue in scope. osv-scanner and semgrep were not installed.
methodology.verification: Every candidate was checked by a fresh verifier agent that did not see the finder's reasoning; one rejection was reviewed and overruled ({ref:storage}).
